question: In which of the following articles, "Right against Exploitation" are mentioned?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Article 23 – 24.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Right against Exploitation is guaranteed by Articles 23 and 24 of the Constitution, in Part III (Fundamental Rights).

◦ Article 23 – Prohibition of traffic in human beings, begar (forced labour) and other similar forms of forced labour; any contravention is a punishable offence.

◦ Article 24 – Prohibition of the employment of children below 14 years of age in any factory, mine or other hazardous employment.

• Laws passed to give effect to these Articles include the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976, the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 and the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• The other Fundamental Rights: Right to Equality (14–18), Right to Freedom (19–22), Right to Freedom of Religion (25–28), Cultural and Educational Rights (29–30) and Right to Constitutional Remedies (32–35).

• Article 21A, added by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002, makes education a Fundamental Right for children aged 6 to 14 years.

NOTE

• Article 23 permits the State to impose compulsory service for public purposes (such as military or social service), provided it makes no discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste or class.

• Fundamental Duties were added as Article 51A by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee.

question: The western cyclonic disturbances in India are brought in by the westerly flow from which region?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Mediterranean region.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Western cyclonic disturbances (Western Disturbances) are extra-tropical storms that originate in the Mediterranean region and are carried into India by the westerly jet stream during the winter months.

◦ They bring light to moderate rainfall (mahawat) to the north-western plains and snowfall to the western Himalayas.

◦ This winter rainfall is extremely important for the rabi crops, especially wheat.

◦ They affect mainly Jammu & Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Delhi and western Uttar Pradesh.

◦ Their intensity and frequency decrease as they move eastwards.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• India's four seasons as per the IMD: Cold weather (December–February), Hot weather (March–May), Advancing south-west monsoon (June–September) and Retreating monsoon (October–November).

• The north-east monsoon brings winter rain to the Coromandel Coast (Tamil Nadu) during October–December.

NOTE

• Local storms: Kalbaisakhi/Nor'westers (West Bengal and Assam), Loo (hot dry wind of northern India), Mango showers (Kerala and Karnataka) and Blossom showers (coffee-growing areas).

• The India Meteorological Department (IMD) was founded in 1875 and is headquartered in New Delhi.

question: Which organisation is responsible for the development and maintenance of the roads on the Indian borders?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Border Roads Organisation.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Border Roads Organisation (BRO) is responsible for the development and maintenance of roads in the border areas of India.

◦ It was established on 7 May 1960 and functions under the Ministry of Defence (since 2015).

◦ Its motto is "Shramena Sarvam Sadhyam" — Everything is achievable through hard work.

◦ It builds and maintains roads in the northern and north-eastern border regions, improving both defence preparedness and socio-economic development of remote areas.

◦ Notable achievements: the Atal Tunnel at Rohtang (opened 2020, the world's longest highway tunnel above 10,000 ft), the Umling La pass road (the world's highest motorable road) and roads in Ladakh and Arunachal Pradesh.

◦ The BRO also undertakes projects in friendly foreign countries such as Bhutan, Myanmar, Afghanistan and Tajikistan.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Roads in India are classified as National Highways, State Highways, District Roads, Rural Roads (PMGSY), Border Roads and International Highways.

• National Highways are built and maintained by the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI), set up in 1988 (operational 1995).

• NH-44 (Srinagar to Kanyakumari) is the longest national highway in India.

NOTE

• The Golden Quadrilateral connects Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata; the North-South and East-West Corridors connect Srinagar–Kanyakumari and Silchar–Porbandar.

• India has the second largest road network in the world after the USA.

question: Who is the author of the epic poem 'Padmavat'?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Malik Muhammad Jayasi.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Padmavat" is an epic poem written by the Sufi poet Malik Muhammad Jayasi in 1540 CE, in the Awadhi dialect of Hindi, using the Persian script.

◦ It narrates the legend of Rani Padmini (Padmavati) of Chittor and the siege of Chittor by Alauddin Khilji in 1303.

◦ It is written in the Masnavi style and belongs to the tradition of Sufi Premakhyan (love-allegory) poetry, in which the love story carries a mystical meaning.

◦ Jayasi lived during the reign of Sher Shah Suri.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Kalidasa, the great Sanskrit poet and dramatist of the Gupta age, wrote Abhijnanashakuntalam, Meghadutam, Raghuvamsham, Kumarasambhavam and Vikramorvashiyam.

• Al-Biruni, who came to India with Mahmud of Ghazni, wrote "Kitab-ul-Hind (Tahqiq-i-Hind)" in Arabic.

• Kuldip Nayar was a well-known Indian journalist and author of "Beyond the Lines".

NOTE

• Other important medieval works: Prithviraj Raso – Chand Bardai; Ramcharitmanas – Tulsidas; Ain-i-Akbari and Akbarnama – Abul Fazl; Tuzuk-i-Baburi – Babur; Humayun Nama – Gulbadan Begum.

• Amir Khusrau, called the "Parrot of India", is credited with developing the Khari Boli and the qawwali form.

question: Density of population, is expressed as __________ .
option_1: number of rural persons per unit area
option_2: number of literate persons per unit area
option_3: number of persons per unit area
option_4: number of animals and persons per unit area
solution_text:
The correct answer is number of persons per unit area.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Population density is defined as the number of persons living per unit area, usually expressed as persons per square kilometre.

◦ Formula: Population Density = Total Population ÷ Total Area (in sq km)

◦ It shows how crowded a place is and is an important measure of the pressure of population on land and resources.

• As per Census 2011:

◦ India's population density = 382 persons per sq km (up from 325 in 2001).

◦ Bihar had the highest density among States (1,106), followed by West Bengal and Kerala.

◦ Arunachal Pradesh had the lowest density (17).

◦ Delhi (11,320) was the highest among Union Territories, and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands (46) the lowest.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Physiological density is the number of persons per unit of cultivable land, and agricultural density is the number of farmers per unit of cultivable land.

• Factors affecting population distribution: relief, climate, soil, water availability, minerals, industrialisation, urbanisation and government policy.

NOTE

• India has about 2.4% of the world's land area but supports around 17-18% of the world's population.

• Census 2011 other figures: population 121.09 crore, sex ratio 943, literacy 74.04%, decadal growth 17.7%.

question: The ______ is a meeting of all adults who live in the area covered by a Panchayat.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Gram Sabha.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Gram Sabha is the assembly of all adult members (registered voters) of a village or group of villages covered by a Gram Panchayat.

◦ It is the only permanent unit in the Panchayati Raj system and is often called the foundation of grassroots democracy.

◦ Article 243A of the Constitution provides that the Gram Sabha may exercise such powers and perform such functions at the village level as the State Legislature may provide by law.

◦ Its functions include approving the annual budget and plans of the Panchayat, selecting beneficiaries of welfare schemes, and conducting social audits (as under MGNREGA).

◦ The Gram Panchayat is the executive body elected by the Gram Sabha, headed by the Sarpanch/Pradhan.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• The 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992 (effective 24 April 1993) gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj, adding Part IX (Articles 243–243O) and the Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects).

◦ It provides for a three-tier system — Gram Panchayat (village), Panchayat Samiti (block) and Zila Parishad (district) — in states with a population above 20 lakh.

◦ It reserves one-third of seats for women and provides a five-year term.

• The 74th Amendment Act, 1992 deals with urban local bodies (municipalities) — Part IXA and the Twelfth Schedule (18 subjects).

NOTE

• The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) recommended the three-tier Panchayati Raj system; Rajasthan (Nagaur, 2 October 1959) was the first state to adopt it, followed by Andhra Pradesh.

• The Ashok Mehta Committee (1977) recommended a two-tier system.

question: Alla Rakha left home at age 12 to learn a musical instrument under the great master (ustad) Mian Qadir Baksh. He became a renowned player of ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Tabla.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Ustad Alla Rakha Khan (1919–2000) was one of the greatest tabla players of Hindustani classical music.

◦ He learned under Ustad Mian Qadir Baksh of the Punjab gharana of tabla.

◦ He became world-famous as the accompanist of Pandit Ravi Shankar, and their performances at Woodstock (1969) and the Concert for Bangladesh (1971) introduced Indian rhythm to Western audiences.

◦ He was awarded the Padma Shri (1977) and the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award (1982).

◦ His son Ustad Zakir Hussain is the leading tabla maestro of the present generation.

• The tabla is an Avanaddha Vadya (membranophone) consisting of two drums — the dayan (treble) and the bayan (bass).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Sarod – Ustad Amjad Ali Khan, Ustad Ali Akbar Khan; Sarangi – Pandit Ram Narayan, Ustad Sultan Khan; Sitar – Pandit Ravi Shankar, Ustad Vilayat Khan.

• The invention of the tabla is traditionally attributed to Amir Khusrau.

• Gharanas of tabla: Delhi, Ajrada, Lucknow, Farukhabad, Benaras and Punjab.

NOTE

• Classification of Indian instruments: Tata Vadya (string), Sushira Vadya (wind), Avanaddha Vadya (membrane percussion) and Ghana Vadya (solid percussion).

• Rhythmic cycles in Hindustani music are called taal — for example Teentaal (16 beats), Jhaptaal (10) and Ektaal (12).

question: When was the Treaty of Purandar signed between Jai Singh I, commander of the Mughal Empire, and Shivaji?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1665.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Treaty of Purandar was signed in June 1665 between Raja Jai Singh I of Amber, the Mughal commander sent by Aurangzeb, and Chhatrapati Shivaji.

• Main terms of the treaty:

◦ Shivaji had to surrender 23 of his 35 forts to the Mughals, keeping only 12, including Raigad.

◦ He agreed to pay tribute and to assist the Mughals in the Deccan.

◦ His son Sambhaji was granted a mansab of 5,000.

◦ Shivaji later visited Agra in 1666, where he was insulted and detained by Aurangzeb, but made his famous escape hidden in a basket of sweets.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Shivaji (1630–1680) was crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad in 1674, with Gaga Bhatt performing the ceremony.

• He killed the Bijapur general Afzal Khan in 1659 at Pratapgarh, and raided the Mughal port of Surat in 1664 and again in 1670.

• His administration was run by a council of eight ministers, the Ashta Pradhan, headed by the Peshwa; his revenue levies were Chauth (25%) and Sardeshmukhi (10%).

NOTE

• After Shivaji, the Maratha throne passed to Sambhaji, Rajaram and Shahu, and real power later moved to the Peshwas of Pune.

• The Maratha state finally ended with the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817–18).

question: Who among the following was named as the captain for the three-match T20 series in New Zealand in November 2022 by Board of Control for Cricket in India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Hardik Pandya.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Hardik Pandya was named by the BCCI as the captain of the Indian team for the three-match T20I series in New Zealand in November 2022.

◦ The senior players were rested after the ICC Men's T20 World Cup 2022 in Australia, and a younger side was sent under his leadership.

◦ Shikhar Dhawan was named captain for the ODI leg of the same tour.

• About Hardik Pandya:

◦ He is an all-rounder from Gujarat and led Gujarat Titans to the IPL title in 2022 in their debut season.

◦ He was part of India's T20 World Cup-winning and Champions Trophy squads in later years.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• The BCCI (Board of Control for Cricket in India) was founded in 1928 and is headquartered at the Wankhede Stadium, Mumbai.

• The ICC (International Cricket Council), founded in 1909, has its headquarters in Dubai, UAE.

• India won the first T20 World Cup in 2007 under M. S. Dhoni, and the ODI World Cup in 1983 (Kapil Dev) and 2011 (Dhoni).

NOTE

• Domestic cricket trophies of India: Ranji Trophy (first-class), Duleep Trophy, Irani Cup, Vijay Hazare Trophy (one-day) and Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy (T20).

• The Indian Premier League (IPL) was started in 2008.

question: Provisions related to the seat of the "Supreme Court of India" is mentioned in which article?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Article 130.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Article 130 of the Constitution deals with the seat of the Supreme Court.

◦ It provides that the Supreme Court shall sit in Delhi or in such other place or places as the Chief Justice of India may, with the approval of the President, appoint.

• Other important Articles relating to the Supreme Court:

◦ Article 124 – Establishment and constitution of the Supreme Court.

◦ Article 129 – The Supreme Court is a Court of Record with the power to punish for contempt.

◦ Article 131 – Original jurisdiction (disputes between the Centre and States, or between States).

◦ Article 132–134 – Appellate jurisdiction in constitutional, civil and criminal cases.

◦ Article 136 – Special Leave Petition (SLP).

◦ Article 137 – Review of its own judgments.

◦ Article 143 – Advisory jurisdiction — the President may seek the Court's opinion.

◦ Article 141 – Law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts in India.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• The Supreme Court of India was inaugurated on 28 January 1950; it replaced the Federal Court of India (1937) and the Privy Council.

• The original strength was 8 judges (1 CJI + 7); it is now 34 (1 CJI + 33).

• The first Chief Justice of India was Justice H. J. Kania.

NOTE

• A Supreme Court judge holds office until the age of 65 years; a High Court judge until 62 years.

• Judges are removed by the process of impeachment under Article 124(4) on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.

question: In 1867, Keshab Chunder Sen helped found the Prarthana Samaj in ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bombay.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Prarthana Samaj was founded in 1867 at Bombay (present-day Mumbai) by Atmaram Pandurang, with the active encouragement and help of Keshab Chandra Sen of the Brahmo Samaj.

• It was a socio-religious reform movement of Western India, working for:

◦ The abolition of caste distinctions and untouchability.

◦ Widow remarriage and women's education.

◦ Raising the age of marriage for both boys and girls.

• Its most prominent leaders were Mahadev Govind Ranade (its guiding spirit), R. G. Bhandarkar and N. G. Chandavarkar.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• The Brahmo Samaj was founded at Calcutta in 1828 by Raja Ram Mohan Roy; Keshab Chandra Sen later led the Brahmo Samaj of India.

• The Arya Samaj was founded at Bombay in 1875 by Swami Dayanand Saraswati, who gave the slogan "Back to the Vedas".

• The Ramakrishna Mission was founded in 1897 by Swami Vivekananda.

• M. G. Ranade also founded the Widow Marriage Association and the Indian National Social Conference (1887).

NOTE

• Raja Ram Mohan Roy is called the "Father of the Indian Renaissance"; the abolition of Sati in 1829 by Lord William Bentinck owed much to his campaign.

• The Native Marriage Act (Civil Marriage Act) of 1872, which legalised inter-caste marriage, was largely the result of Keshab Chandra Sen's efforts.

question: Which dancer received the Padma Shri award in 2021 for her contribution to art?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Manjamma Jogati.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Matha B. Manjamma Jogati received the Padma Shri in 2021 for her contribution to art.

◦ She is a renowned exponent of the Jogati Nritya, a traditional folk dance form of North Karnataka associated with the worship of Goddess Yellamma (Renuka).

◦ She is a transgender folk artist and became the President of the Karnataka Janapada Academy — the first from her community to hold that office.

◦ Her recognition is regarded as a landmark for folk art and for social inclusion.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Alarmel Valli is a celebrated Bharatanatyam dancer of the Pandanallur style; she received the Padma Shri (1991) and the Padma Bhushan (2004).

• The Padma Awards — Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan and Padma Shri — were instituted in 1954 and are announced every year on the eve of Republic Day.

◦ Padma Vibhushan – exceptional and distinguished service; Padma Bhushan – distinguished service of a high order; Padma Shri – distinguished service in any field.

NOTE

• The Bharat Ratna is India's highest civilian award, instituted in 1954; its first recipients were Dr. S. Radhakrishnan, C. Rajagopalachari and C. V. Raman.

• Folk dances of Karnataka: Yakshagana, Dollu Kunitha, Veeragase, Kamsale and Jogati Nritya.

question: ______ is celebrated as the New Year of Kerala.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Vishu.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Vishu is celebrated as the New Year of Kerala, falling in the month of Medam (mid-April), usually on 14 or 15 April.

◦ It marks the sun's transit into Medam rashi (Aries) and the beginning of the astronomical new year.

◦ Its central ritual is the "Vishukkani" — an auspicious arrangement of rice, fruits, golden konna (kanikonna) flowers, coins, a mirror and an image of Lord Krishna, which is the first thing seen on waking on Vishu morning.

◦ Elders give money to the young as "Vishukkaineettam", and a grand feast, the Vishu Sadya, is prepared.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Onam is the great harvest festival of Kerala, celebrated in the month of Chingam to welcome the mythical king Mahabali; its features include the Pookalam (floral carpet), Vallamkali (snake-boat race) and Onam Sadya.

• Pongal is the harvest festival of Tamil Nadu, celebrated in January; Bonalu is a festival of Telangana dedicated to Goddess Mahakali.

NOTE

• New Year festivals across India on roughly the same days in April: Baisakhi (Punjab), Bihu/Rongali Bihu (Assam), Poila Boishakh (West Bengal), Puthandu (Tamil Nadu), Ugadi (Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh) and Gudi Padwa (Maharashtra, in March–April).

• Kerala's capital is Thiruvananthapuram; its classical dances are Kathakali and Mohiniyattam.

question: The Bandipur National Park is located in which of the following states?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Karnataka.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Bandipur National Park is located in the Chamarajanagar district of Karnataka, in the Western Ghats.

◦ It was established as a national park in 1974 and was among the first nine tiger reserves created under Project Tiger (1973).

◦ It lies at the junction of the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve, adjoining Nagarhole (Karnataka), Mudumalai (Tamil Nadu) and Wayanad (Kerala) — together forming India's largest habitat for wild elephants.

◦ Key species: tiger, Indian elephant, gaur, sloth bear, dhole (wild dog) and sambar.

◦ The Kabini river separates Bandipur from Nagarhole.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Other national parks of Karnataka: Nagarhole (Rajiv Gandhi), Bannerghatta, Kudremukh and Anshi.

• Project Tiger was launched in 1973, and the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) was set up in 2005-06.

• The Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve was India's first biosphere reserve (1986).

NOTE

• Jim Corbett National Park (Uttarakhand, 1936) is India's oldest national park.

• The Western Ghats are one of India's four biodiversity hotspots and a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2012).

question: Duties levied on goods produced within the country are ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is excise taxes.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Excise duty is a tax levied on goods produced or manufactured within the country.

◦ It is an indirect tax, since the burden can be shifted from the manufacturer to the consumer.

◦ It was earlier known as Central Excise Duty or CENVAT and was levied by the Union Government.

◦ Since 1 July 2017, most excise duties have been subsumed into the Goods and Services Tax (GST); excise duty now continues mainly on petroleum products, tobacco and alcohol (state excise).

• Customs duty, by contrast, is levied on goods imported into or exported out of the country.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Anti-dumping duty is imposed on imported goods sold below their normal price, to protect domestic producers from unfair competition.

• Wealth tax was a direct tax on the net wealth of individuals; it was abolished in India in 2015.

• Direct taxes (income tax, corporation tax) cannot be shifted; indirect taxes (GST, customs, excise) can be shifted to the consumer.

NOTE

• GST was introduced on 1 July 2017 through the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016; its slogan is "One Nation, One Tax, One Market".

◦ The GST Council (Article 279A) is chaired by the Union Finance Minister.

◦ GST has four slabs — 5%, 12%, 18% and 28%; petroleum products and alcohol are outside its ambit.

• CBDT administers direct taxes and CBIC indirect taxes.

question: The ozone layer is found in which of the following layers of the atmosphere?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Stratosphere.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The ozone layer (ozonosphere) is found in the stratosphere, at a height of roughly 15 to 35 km above the earth's surface.

◦ Ozone (O₃) absorbs the sun's harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation, protecting life on earth from skin cancer, cataracts and damage to crops — it is therefore called the "protective umbrella of the earth".

• Layers of the atmosphere, from the surface upwards:

◦ Troposphere (up to about 8–18 km) – all weather phenomena occur here; temperature falls with height (normal lapse rate 6.5°C per km).

◦ Stratosphere (up to about 50 km) – contains the ozone layer; ideal for jet aircraft, as it is free of turbulence.

◦ Mesosphere (up to about 80 km) – meteors burn up here; the coldest layer.

◦ Thermosphere / Ionosphere – radio waves are reflected back to earth from here; auroras occur in this layer.

◦ Exosphere – the outermost layer, merging into space.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• The ozone hole over Antarctica was discovered in 1985; CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons) are the main ozone-depleting substances.

• The Montreal Protocol (1987) was adopted to phase out ozone-depleting substances; World Ozone Day is observed on 16 September.

NOTE

• The atmosphere is composed of about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and small amounts of argon, carbon dioxide and other gases.

• Greenhouse gases — carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, water vapour and CFCs — cause global warming, a separate phenomenon from ozone depletion.

question: Who among the following was the Governor-General from 1773 to 1785?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Warren Hastings.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Warren Hastings was the first Governor-General of Bengal, holding office from 1773 to 1785 under the Regulating Act of 1773.

• Key facts about his administration:

◦ He abolished the Dual Government in Bengal introduced by Robert Clive.

◦ The Supreme Court at Calcutta was established in 1774 under the same Act.

◦ He founded the Calcutta Madrasa (1781), and Sir William Jones founded the Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784) during his tenure.

◦ He fought the First Anglo-Maratha War, ended by the Treaty of Salbai (1782), and the Second Anglo-Mysore War.

◦ He was impeached in the British Parliament (1788–1795) on charges of corruption, notably in the Rohilla War and the cases of Nand Kumar, Chait Singh of Benaras and the Begums of Awadh; he was finally acquitted.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Lord William Bentinck (1828–35) was the first Governor-General of India (under the Charter Act of 1833); he abolished Sati (1829) and suppressed Thugee.

• Lord Dalhousie (1848–56) introduced the Doctrine of Lapse, the railways (1853), the telegraph and the postal system.

• Lord Mountbatten was the last Viceroy of British India and the first Governor-General of independent India.

NOTE

• The Regulating Act, 1773 was the first step by the British Parliament to regulate the East India Company's affairs; Pitt's India Act, 1784 established the Board of Control.

• Lord Canning was the last Governor-General and the first Viceroy of India (1858).

question: The Tapu dance from Arunachal Pradesh is performed by members of the ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Adi Tribe.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Tapu dance is a traditional war dance of the Adi tribe of Arunachal Pradesh.

◦ It is performed by men, who carry swords, shields and spears, and it depicts scenes of war and valour.

◦ The dancers wear traditional warrior costume with helmets, and the dance is accompanied by war cries and drum beats.

• The Adi are one of the largest tribes of Arunachal Pradesh; their main festival is Solung, and another well-known dance of theirs is the Ponung.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Other major tribes of Arunachal Pradesh: Nyishi (the largest), Apatani, Monpa, Galo, Mishmi, Tagin and Wancho.

• Festivals of Arunachal Pradesh: Solung (Adi), Losar (Monpa), Nyokum (Nyishi), Myoko and Dree (Apatani) and Mopin (Galo).

• The Munda tribe belongs to Jharkhand, while the Damor and Garasia tribes are found in Rajasthan and Gujarat.

NOTE

• Arunachal Pradesh became a full-fledged State on 20 February 1987; its capital is Itanagar and it is called the "Land of the Rising Sun" or "Orchid State of India".

• Tawang Monastery in Arunachal Pradesh is the largest monastery in India.

question: The iron pillar is situated in which of the following places?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Delhi.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The famous Iron Pillar stands in the Qutub Minar complex at Mehrauli, Delhi.

◦ It is about 7.2 metres (24 feet) high and weighs over 6 tonnes.

◦ It is famous for its rust-resistant composition, which has kept it free of corrosion for more than 1,600 years — a remarkable achievement of ancient Indian metallurgy.

◦ The resistance is due to a protective film of misawite, formed because of the high phosphorus content and the absence of sulphur and magnesium in the iron.

◦ It bears a Sanskrit inscription in Brahmi script referring to a king named Chandra, generally identified with Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya) of the Gupta dynasty.

◦ It was originally erected elsewhere (possibly at Udayagiri) and later shifted to Delhi.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• The Qutub Minar complex also contains the Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque, the Alai Darwaza (built by Alauddin Khilji, 1311) and the tomb of Iltutmish; it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1993).

• Qutub Minar was begun by Qutb-ud-din Aibak and completed by Iltutmish; it is the tallest brick minaret in the world (72.5 m).

NOTE

• The Gupta age is called the "Golden Age of India" for its achievements in art, literature, science and metallurgy.

• Delhi's three UNESCO World Heritage Sites are the Qutub Minar complex, Humayun's Tomb and the Red Fort complex.

question: LPG subsidy to domestic consumer under PAHAL Scheme is given by ______.
option_1: Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas
option_2: Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The PAHAL scheme (Pratyaksh Hanstantarit Labh), also called DBTL (Direct Benefit Transfer for LPG), is run by the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas.

◦ It was launched on 1 June 2013, modified and re-launched on 15 November 2014, and rolled out across the country from 1 January 2015.

◦ Under it, the consumer buys the LPG cylinder at the market price, and the subsidy is transferred directly into his or her bank account.

◦ Objectives: to eliminate diversion and duplicate connections, to remove ghost beneficiaries, and to ensure the subsidy reaches the genuine user.

◦ It is linked to Aadhaar and the bank account (the JAM trinity — Jan Dhan, Aadhaar, Mobile).

◦ PAHAL entered the Guinness Book of World Records as the largest direct benefit transfer scheme in the world.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• The "GiveItUp" campaign, launched in 2015, encouraged well-off consumers to voluntarily surrender their LPG subsidy, which was then used to give free connections to poor households.

• The Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana (PMUY), launched on 1 May 2016 from Ballia, Uttar Pradesh, provides free LPG connections to women of BPL households; its slogan is "Swachh Indhan, Behtar Jeevan".

NOTE

• LPG (Liquefied Petroleum Gas) consists mainly of butane and propane; ethyl mercaptan is added to give it a smell so leaks can be detected.

• Ministry–scheme pairs: Ujjwala and PAHAL – Petroleum and Natural Gas; PM-KISAN – Agriculture; MGNREGA – Rural Development; PMAY-U and PM SVANidhi – Housing and Urban Affairs.

question: Who among the following Navratnas from Chandragupta II court wrote 'Mantrashastra'?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Vetala Bhatta.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Vetala Bhatta was one of the Navratnas (nine gems) in the court of Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya) and is traditionally credited with the work "Mantrashastra" (also known as the Niti-pradipa, a treatise on statecraft and policy).

• The nine gems (Navratnas) of Chandragupta II's court were:

◦ Kalidasa – the greatest Sanskrit poet and dramatist (Abhijnanashakuntalam, Meghadutam, Raghuvamsham, Kumarasambhavam).

◦ Amarasimha – lexicographer, author of the Sanskrit thesaurus Amarakosha.

◦ Varahamihira – astronomer, author of Brihat Samhita, Panchasiddhantika and Brihat Jataka.

◦ Dhanvantari – physician, associated with Ayurveda.

◦ Kshapanaka, Shanku, Ghatakarpara, Vararuchi and Vetala Bhatta.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Chandragupta II defeated the Shakas and took the title Shakari; he also used the title Vikramaditya.

◦ The Chinese pilgrim Fa-Hien visited India during his reign (c. 399–414 CE).

◦ The Mehrauli Iron Pillar inscription refers to a king Chandra, generally identified with him.

• Aryabhata, author of the Aryabhatiya, and Brahmagupta also belong to the Gupta age.

NOTE

• The Gupta rulers in order: Sri Gupta → Ghatotkacha → Chandragupta I → Samudragupta → Chandragupta II → Kumaragupta I → Skandagupta.

• Samudragupta is called the "Napoleon of India"; the Allahabad Pillar Inscription (Prayag Prashasti) by Harisena records his conquests.

question: Fatima Sheikh was widely regarded as ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is India's First Female Muslim Teacher.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Fatima Sheikh (born 9 January 1831) is widely regarded as India's first Muslim woman teacher.

◦ She was a close associate of Jyotiba Phule and Savitribai Phule, and worked with them in the cause of education for girls and the depressed classes.

◦ When the Phules were forced to leave their home for their reform work, Fatima Sheikh and her brother Usman Sheikh gave them shelter, and the first school was run from their house in 1848 at Pune.

◦ She taught in the schools of the Native Female School, Pune and the Society for Promoting the Education of Mahars, Mangs and Others.

◦ Google honoured her with a Doodle on 9 January 2022, on her 191st birth anniversary.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Savitribai Phule is regarded as India's first woman teacher and a pioneer of women's education; she and Jyotiba opened the first school for girls in 1848.

• Anandibai Joshi and Kadambini Ganguly were among India's first women doctors (1886).

• Jyotiba Phule founded the Satyashodhak Samaj (1873) and wrote Gulamgiri.

NOTE

• Other pioneering Indian women: Sarojini Naidu – first woman President of the INC (1925) and first woman Governor; Indira Gandhi – first woman Prime Minister; Pratibha Patil – first woman President; Kiran Bedi – first woman IPS officer; Kalpana Chawla – first Indian-born woman in space.

question: Who was the only Indian to qualify for the 2022 Winter Olympics?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Arif Mohammad Khan.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Arif Mohammad Khan (Arif Khan), an alpine skier from Jammu and Kashmir, was the only Indian athlete to qualify for the 2022 Winter Olympics held at Beijing, China.

◦ He qualified in two events — the Slalom and the Giant Slalom — becoming the first Indian to qualify directly in two events at a Winter Olympics.

◦ He was India's flag-bearer at the opening ceremony of the Beijing 2022 Games.

◦ He hails from Baramulla district, in the Gulmarg region of Jammu and Kashmir.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Shiva Keshavan is India's best-known luge athlete, who represented the country at six consecutive Winter Olympics before retiring.

• Himanshu Thakur (alpine skiing) and Nadeem Iqbal (cross-country skiing) represented India at earlier Winter Games.

• The Beijing 2022 Winter Olympics made Beijing the first city to host both the Summer (2008) and Winter Olympics.

NOTE

• The first Winter Olympics were held at Chamonix, France, in 1924; the Winter and Summer Games have been held in alternate even years since 1994.

• The International Olympic Committee (IOC) is headquartered at Lausanne, Switzerland; Milan-Cortina, Italy, hosted the 2026 Winter Olympics.

question: Which of the following is a non-metal that can exist in different form?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Carbon.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Carbon is a non-metal that exists in several different forms, called allotropes — different physical forms of the same element in the same physical state.

• The main allotropes of carbon:

◦ Diamond – the hardest natural substance; each carbon atom is bonded to four others in a rigid three-dimensional network; it is a bad conductor of electricity but an excellent conductor of heat.

◦ Graphite – soft and slippery, with carbon atoms in layers; it is a good conductor of electricity and is used in pencils, electrodes and as a lubricant.

◦ Fullerene (Buckminsterfullerene, C₆₀) – a football-shaped molecule, discovered in 1985.

◦ Others include graphene, carbon nanotubes, charcoal, coke and lampblack.

• Remarkably, diamond and graphite are chemically identical — both are pure carbon — yet differ completely in properties because of their different atomic arrangements.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature; Lithium is the lightest metal; Potassium is a highly reactive alkali metal — all three are metals, not non-metals.

• Other elements showing allotropy: sulphur (rhombic, monoclinic, plastic), phosphorus (white, red, black) and oxygen (O₂ and ozone O₃).

NOTE

• Carbon has atomic number 6 and forms the basis of organic chemistry, since it shows catenation (self-linking) and tetravalency.

• Carbon dating (C-14) is used to determine the age of fossils and archaeological remains.

question: The innermost part of a flower is called the ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is pistil.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The pistil (or carpel) is the innermost part of a flower and forms the female reproductive organ, collectively known as the gynoecium.

◦ It has three parts: the stigma (the sticky top that receives pollen), the style (the tube connecting stigma to ovary) and the ovary (which contains the ovules).

◦ After fertilisation, the ovary develops into the fruit and the ovules into seeds.

• The four whorls of a typical flower, from the outside inwards, are:

◦ Calyx (sepals) – the outermost whorl, usually green, protecting the bud.

◦ Corolla (petals) – brightly coloured, attracting pollinators.

◦ Androecium (stamens) – the male reproductive organ, each stamen having an anther (producing pollen) and a filament.

◦ Gynoecium (pistil/carpel) – the innermost whorl, the female reproductive organ.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• A flower with all four whorls is complete; one having both stamens and pistil is bisexual (hibiscus, mustard), while unisexual flowers have only one (papaya, watermelon).

• Pollination is the transfer of pollen from anther to stigma — self-pollination (same flower) or cross-pollination (different flowers), carried out by wind, water, insects or birds.

• Fertilisation is the fusion of the male and female gametes to form a zygote.

NOTE

• In flowering plants (angiosperms), double fertilisation takes place — one male gamete fuses with the egg and the other with the polar nuclei to form the endosperm.

• Gymnosperms (pine, cycas) bear naked seeds and have no fruit.
